collection.title: Trajectory fit alone does not identify causal edges: a white-box masked ODE benchmark for trans-omics digital twins of drug action mechanisms
collection.authors: Zhang, Z.; Jia, L.; Pan, Y.; Zhao, H.
collection.author_corresponding_institution: China Academy of Chinese Medical Sciences
collection.abstract: Dynamic multi-omics models infer drug mechanisms from trajectories, but trajectory accuracy alone cannot verify that learned regulatory edges are mechanistically correct. We asked to what extent fitting time-series dynamics identifies intervenable causal edges across observation and optimization budgets.We built white-box ordinary differential equations with candidate-edge masks for gene-expression, protein, signalling and metabolite dynamics, using a mouse-liver trans-omics topology and ground-truth semi-synthetic time series. Under noise-free,complete, densely sampled data, from-scratch training ranked edges near chance(edge-class area under the receiver-operating characteristic curve, 0.48-0.53); the unattainable oracle-initialized upper bound reached 0.94-0.99 on the same metric.Unobserved layers absorbed error. In ground-truth knockout tests, development-batch endpoint-sign accuracy was 67.9% for one-hop non-convergent targets but 33.3% for two-hop targets. Across tested practical budgets, fitting did not yield reliable edge recovery; trajectory fit alone therefore does not establish mechanistic identification. This benchmark supports mechanistic audits and exploratory per-prediction confidence grading in multi-omics models.

collection.title: Comparative Mitogenomics and Molecular Phylogeny of Agriculturally Significant Tephritid Fruit Fly Pests in Bangladesh
collection.authors: Rahman, S.; Shormi, F. A.
collection.abstract: Tephritid fruit flies of the tribe Dacini rank among the most economically destructive agricultural pests globally, with several species of Bactrocera Macquart and Zeugodacus Hendel causing severe losses to fruit and vegetable production across South and Southeast Asia. Bangladesh harbors several economically important dacine species, including Bactrocera dorsalis (Hendel), B. carambolae (Drew & Hancock), B. zonata (Saunders), B. correcta (Bezzi) and Zeugodacus cucurbitae (Coquillett). Here we present a comparative mitogenomic and phylogenetic framework based on 21 unique GenBank mitogenome records: 19 dacine ingroup records and two outgroups. The ingroup includes B. papayae, B. philippinensis and B. invadens, whose synonymy with B. dorsalis is disputed. All records contained 13 protein-coding genes (PCGs) and two rRNA genes. Genome size in the 14 taxa of subgenus Bactrocera ranged from 15,273 to 15,977 bp. Whole-genome AT content ranged from 66.6% in B. tsuneonis to 82.2% in Drosophila melanogaster, and the five focal pest species clustered at 72.9-73.6%. Maximum-likelihood analysis of a 13,600-site alignment (13 PCGs plus 12S and 16S rRNA; GTR+FO; IQ-TREE v1.6.11; 1,000 ultrafast bootstrap replicates, UFBoot) recovered the B. dorsalis complex (UFBoot = 100), within which pairwise distances were only 0.64-1.33%, and a B. correcta + B. zonata pair (UFBoot = 100). Nine taxa showed compositional heterogeneity and third codon positions were highly variable, so deeper nodes should be interpreted cautiously. As no Bangladeshi specimens were sequenced, this study is a curated reference baseline for molecular identification and pest surveillance, not a population-genomic analysis.

collection.title: Effects of different shading levels on growth, physiology and leaf surface micromorphology of Sorbus sibirica "Dong Hong" seedlings
collection.authors: Huang, R.; Gong, W.; Li, X.; Ji, S.; Cui, T.; Zhang, L.
collection.abstract: Background: Shading may influence nursery cultivation of Sorbus sibirica "Dong Hong", but its growth and physiological responses remain insufficiently characterised. Aims: To assess seedling responses to shading and inform container nursery management. Methods: One-year-old potted seedlings were grown under full sunlight (CK) and nominal shading levels of 30% (L1), 50% (L2) and 70% (L3) for 100 days in Qiqihar, China. Growth, biomass allocation, root morphology, physiological traits and leaf micromorphology were assessed. Results: Seedling height, total biomass, chlorophyll and soluble protein contents peaked under L1, whereas basal diameter and invertase activity declined with increasing shade. Under L1, total root length and mean root diameter were comparable to CK, but root tip number and root volume were lower. Root biomass proportion remained similar across treatments. L2 and L3 had higher leaf biomass proportions but lower total biomass than CK. Shaded seedlings had smaller stomatal dimensions. Biomass and root morphological values were lowest under L3. Conclusions: L1 combined greater biomass with thinner stems and altered root morphology. Restricted rooting volume, limited environmental monitoring and a single summer-to-autumn trial warrant validation before extending these findings to other seasons, regions or cultivation systems.

collection.title: Microbes use transporters to regulate the release of metabolites based on value
collection.authors: Sulheim, S.; Broli, G.; Doubleday, P. F.; Gillon, A.; Luneau, J. S.; Padmanabha, P.; Quinn, A.; Ulrich, E.; Vogel, M. A.; Zamboni, N.; Engel, P.; Mitri, S.
collection.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Fundamental Microbiology, University of Lausanne
collection.abstract: Microbial interactions are shaped by the exchange of metabolites, ranging from intermediates in central carbon metabolism to amino acids, vitamins and fermentation by-products. While specific metabolic processes such as overflow metabolism are well documented, a general principle explaining the chemical diversity of metabolite release and the variation in individual release rates remains elusive. Here, using a combination of computational and experimental approaches on seven different microbes, we show that release rates are negatively correlated with the value of metabolites, and that this relationship explains more variability in release rates than other frequently associated factors. By measuring metabolite release from 67 E. coli mutants lacking individual transport genes, we find that transporters both cause and counteract net metabolite release. These findings suggest that metabolite release constitutes a fitness cost that microbes have evolved to reduce, while revealing the underlying transport mechanism. This unifying explanation reshapes our understanding of how microbial interactions emerge and persist.

collection.title: Identification of SAMD4B as a Centrosome-Associated Regulator of the Sonic Hedgehog Signaling Pathway
collection.authors: Bernatik, O.; Vyslouzil, D.; Paclikova, P.; Renzova, T.; Kovarikova, P.; Cajanek, L.
collection.abstract: Background: Many protein-protein interactions are required for the assembly and function of primary cilia, microtubule-based organelles critical for the Sonic hedgehog (Shh) signaling pathway and, in turn, for embryonic development and tissue homeostasis. However, our understanding of this complex process remains incomplete. Methods: To identify new regulators of primary cilia formation or function, we carried out proximity labeling experiments and compared interactomes under ciliogenesis-restrictive and permissive conditions. Using an unbiased strategy, we selected candidates that were tested functionally by siRNA-mediated depletion or gene editing, in combination with gene expression analysis and various microscopy techniques, using either vertebrate cell lines or zebrafish as model systems. Results: We demonstrate that one of our identified candidates, protein SAMD4B, is associated with the centrosome and is required for Shh signaling in NIH3T3 cells and eye development in zebrafish. Our data implicate defective ciliary recruitment of Shh pathway regulators ARL13B and SMO as a plausible mechanism underlying the SAMD4B-mediated regulation of Shh signaling. Conclusions: Together, our data identify a previously unrecognized link between SAMD4B, a protein known to be associated with cytoplasmic RNA condensates, and ciliary signaling.

collection.title: Long-term population monitoring reveals an alarming decline in the endangered endemic Reunion Harrier Circus maillardi
collection.authors: Villers, A.; Cornulier, T.; Eraud, C.; Couturier, T.; Ferret, P.; Chiron, D.; Laurent, N.; Besnard, A.; Bretagnolle, V.; Salamolard, M.; Grondin, V.; Couzi, F.-X.; Fay, R.; Augiron, S.
collection.author_corresponding_institution: Societe d'Etudes Ornithologiques de la Reunion
collection.abstract: Insular species are disproportionately vulnerable to extinction due to small population sizes, geographic isolation, and high susceptibility to stochastic and anthropogenic pressures. The Reunion Harrier Circus maillardi, the last breeding raptor on La Reunion (Indian Ocean), is currently listed as Endangered (EN) on the IUCN Red List, although population decline has so far only been suspected rather than robustly quantified. Concerns have recently emerged regarding the demographic impacts of secondary poisoning from anticoagulant rodenticides used for rat control in agricultural landscapes, in addition to habitat loss, fragmentation, and reduced genetic diversity. Here, we analysed data from three standardised island-wide breeding surveys (1998--2000, 2009--2010, 2017--2019), encompassing 346 sampling points and totalling over 1,500 h of observation, to quantify population trends and their spatial variation. Using generalized additive mixed models accounting for spatial structure and heterogeneous survey designs, we detected a significant decline of -46% [-62%; -27%] in the relative abundance of breeding pairs at the island scale over 21 years, equivalent to three generations, supporting the species' current Endangered status. The decline was steeper between 1998 and 2009 (-33% [-52%; -9%]) than between 2009 and 2017 (-18% [-42%;+14%]). The decrease was more markedly pronounced in the eastern part of the island (-57% [-71%; -40%]) than in the west (-29% [-53%; + 0.8%]), reflecting a complete reversal of the historical east-west abundance gradient. Combined with previous evidence of inbreeding, high mutational load, and rodenticide exposure, these results suggest the population is undergoing an extinction vortex requiring immediate, spatially targeted conservation actions, including reduced rodenticide exposure and genetic management. These findings also underscore the need for sustained monitoring and improved demographic knowledge to support the implementation of the ongoing National Species Action Plan

collection.title: NeuroSim: a clinically informed multi-disorder EEG simulator with personalized pattern injection and AI-driven neurological modeling
collection.authors: Bunterngchit, C.; Aslam, S.; Sattar, A.; Rasool, A.; Wang, Y.
collection.abstract: Deep learning for electroencephalography (EEG) based neurodiagnostics is constrained by the limited availability of labeled clinical recordings. Datasets covering Alzheimers disease (AD), Parkinsons disease (PD), schizophrenia (SCZ), epilepsy (EPI), and frontotemporal dementia (FTD) are scarce, demographically narrow, and heterogeneous across acquisition sites, while privacy requirements restrict data sharing. Existing EEG simulators typically address a single disorder or trade biological interpretability for statistical fidelity. This study presents NeuroSim, a simulation framework that generates synthetic multichannel EEG with user-controlled injection of disease-specific patterns across five disorders and multiple severity levels. A physiologically motivated baseline generator produces band-limited rhythms, event-related potentials, artifacts, and hierarchical subject-level and trial-level variability. Disease patterns are introduced through region-specific and severity-specific spectral modulation that encodes established biomarkers, including posterior alpha suppression in AD, motor beta enhancement in PD, and spike-wave discharges in EPI. An interactive interface exposes montage, sampling rate, duration, artifacts, stimuli, affected regions, and severity, and exports signals with reproducible metadata. The simulated signals reproduced the expected biomarker directionality under spectral, topographic, and multivariate statistical analysis. A convolutional-attention classifier trained on simulated data reached 95.3 to 96.8 percent hold-out accuracy, and post hoc explainability analyses produced class-separable embeddings with attributions concentrated on pathophysiologically expected electrodes. Application of the analysis pipeline to recordings from the Temple University Hospital EEG Corpus confirmed compatibility with heterogeneous clinical data. In subject-level augmentation experiments on real clinical EEG, supplementing real training data with NeuroSim samples increased classification accuracy from 91.6 to 94.5 percent for AD versus healthy controls and from 90.9 to 94.0 percent for PD versus healthy controls, exceeding the improvement obtained with conventional signal-level augmentation. NeuroSim is released as open-source software to support augmentation, benchmarking, and explainable artificial intelligence in neurological diagnostics.

collection.title: Learning RNA secondary structure from chemical probing with MXfold2
collection.authors: Yamauchi, R.; Tsukiyama, S.; Sato, K.
collection.abstract: Training RNA secondary structure predictors is limited by scarce reference annotations, even as chemical probing produces abundant nucleotide-level measurements. These measurements inform pairing states without identifying base-pairing partners. Here we extend MXfold2, which combines neural and thermodynamic folding scores, to learn from probing profiles and predict RNA secondary structures from sequence alone. We introduce three training objectives. One learns from probing-assisted target structures. The other two use implicit maximum-likelihood estimation to pass surrogate gradients from reactivity-ranking and likelihood losses through discrete folding. Simulations, RNAgym measurements and external structural tests show improved chemical agreement and gains in exact base-pair prediction when chemical supervision is combined with structural pretraining and replay. Probing profiles can thus broaden the range of RNAs that inform sequence-only structure prediction, including RNA populations with few complete structure annotations.

collection.title: SNP2Cluster-Py: A pathogen-agnostic, context-aware framework for Core SNP and transmission-cluster analysis
collection.authors: Kwenda, S.; Christoffels, A.
collection.abstract: Whole-genome sequencing enables high-resolution identification of genetically related pathogen isolates, but genomic similarity alone does not establish epidemiologically meaningful transmission. We developed SNP2Cluster-Py, an open-source Python framework that separates context-aware Core SNP clustering from the subsequent application of epidemiological and temporal criteria. The software accepts a precomputed pairwise Core SNP-distance matrix and user-configured metadata and supports analysis of all eligible isolates in a single context, as well as sequence-type, geographical, epidemiological and ordered composite contexts. Within each context, authoritative Core clusters are defined as connected components of an SNP-threshold graph; K-means assignments and silhouette widths are retained as exploratory diagnostics only. We evaluated the workflow using 172 Klebsiella pneumoniae isolates from six neonatal-surveillance hospitals in South Africa, a focused 36-isolate single-hospital subset from the same surveillance dataset, and 168 Streptococcus pneumoniae carriage isolates from Ghana. In the full K. pneumoniae dataset, ST-only analysis assigned 141 isolates to Core SNP clusters, whereas Facility + ST analysis assigned 134, demonstrating how facility stratification can remove cross-facility genomic connections. In the single-hospital subset, both contexts assigned 30 of 36 isolates to five Core clusters, and Facility analysis retained 23 isolates in four temporally compatible clusters. In the pneumococcal dataset, ST-context analysis assigned 114 isolates to 38 Core clusters, which were characterised across sampling locations and time through Community analysis. SNP2Cluster-Py therefore provides a reproducible framework for adapting genomic clustering to specific surveillance questions while maintaining a clear distinction between genomic relatedness, analytically inferred transmission clusters and confirmed direct transmission. SNP2Cluster-Py v1.1.2 is available under the Apache License 2.0 through GitHub and Zenodo.

collection.title: CELL-X: A Single-Cell Transcriptomics Framework for Cell-Type and Disease-State Prioritization of Type 2 Diabetes Risk Genes
collection.authors: Uddin, M. M.; Khan, S. M. Z. A.; Bomma Yadagiri, K.
collection.author_corresponding_institution: A.V. College of Arts, Science & Commerce (Autonomous), Osmania University
collection.abstract: Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified hundreds of loci associated with Type 2 Diabetes (T2D), yet pinpointing specific causal genes and their relevant cellular contexts remains a critical bottleneck. To address this gap, we developed CELL-X, a novel computational framework systematically integrating fine-mapped genetic evidence with high-resolution single-cell transcriptomics and disease progression dynamics. Utilizing a custom out-of-memory processing engine, we analyzed an integrated human pancreatic islet atlas of 245,878 cells without forced data downsampling. We evaluated 37 genetically supported T2D candidate genes, quantifying cell-type relevance via a max-scaled Cell Relevance Score (CRS). Disease-associated transcriptional dynamics were subsequently incorporated using a Disease Relevance Score (DRS) based on heterogeneous expression shifts across normal, prediabetic, and T2D metabolic states. CELL-X successfully identified beta cells as the dominant disease-relevant cellular context and prioritized established causal genes, including SLC30A8, GLIS3, GCK, and TCF7L2. Validation against a 30-gene benchmark demonstrated exceptional target recovery and significant metabolic pathway enrichment. Furthermore, rigorous statistical null modeling confirmed this prioritization is driven by true biological variance rather than background transcriptomic noise. Ultimately, CELL-X provides a highly scalable, robust framework for generating biologically informed hypotheses in complex polygenic disease research.

collection.title: The tumor suppressor role of the KRAS proto-oncogene in metastatic pancreatic cancer.
collection.authors: Zhang, L.; Gurreri, E.; Tang, H.; Bania, A.; Ibrahim, M. J.; Rinaldi, R.; Pandey, A.; Cecchetto, L.; Granato, E.; Khan, H.; Hoang, A.; Catania, D.; Carlino, C.; Marszaleck, J. R.; Shi, C.; Sgambato, A.; Tortora, G.; Carugo, A.; Viale, A.; Cittaro, D.; Sioletic, S.; Wood, L.; Klimstra, D. S.; Basturk, O.; Pant, S.; Javle, M.; Msaouel, P.; Gao, J.; Akdemir, K. C.; Wang, L.; Van Loo, P.; Citron, F.; Heffernan, T.; Iacobuzio-Donahue, C. A.; Kopetz, S.; Perelli, L.; Genovese, G.
collection.abstract: KRAS is the most frequently mutated proto-oncogene in human cancers. Progression to advanced disease is frequently associated with allelic imbalance of the KRAS locus with gain of the mutant allele and loss of the wild-type allele through clonal and sub-clonal loss of heterozygosity (LOH). While a large body of literature has focused on the effects of allelic imbalance on oncogene addiction through gain of the mutant allele, the role of the wild-type KRAS proto-oncogene in malignant progression has not been fully elucidated. To capture this phenomenon, we developed a first-in-class somatic mosaic and lineage tracing genetically engineered mouse model (smGMLT) of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma allowing for real time in vivo tracing of Kras-LOH. Longitudinal characterization of the smGMLT demonstrated the presence of a strong evolutionary bottleneck towards the selective loss of the wild-type allele at metastatic sites. Cross species analysis leveraging research autopsies and surgical specimens revealed that KRAS-LOH is associated with metastatic dissemination and shorter overall survival. Transcriptomic analysis through single-cell RNA sequencing uncovered a conserved phenomenon whereby KRAS-LOH is paralleled by an immune evasive phenotype through loss of the tumor-cell interferon response and reduced CD8+ T cell infiltration. In line with this evidence, orthotopic transplants of isogenic tumor populations differing for the Kras allelic status demonstrated that only cancer cells with Kras-LOH are are able to form tumors in immune competent animals. Restoration of the wild-type allele abrogates tumorigenesis in KrasLOH transplants in immunocompetent through activation of the TBK1-IRF axis. Altogether, these studies demonstrate that the KRAS proto-oncogene is a functional tumor suppressor in pancreatic cancer exerting its function through interferon-mediated, cell-extrinsic modulation of the tumor immune microenvironment.

collection.title: Spatial organization of a SPINK1-associated tumor-stromal ecosystem links metabolic remodeling to immune restriction in bladder cancer
collection.authors: Yu, Q.; Wu, Y.; Han, X.; Lu, Y.; Li, H.; Jiang, Y. D. D.; Zhou, J.; Li, Y.; Huang, H.; Chen, W.; Li, X.; Ye, F.; Zheng, L.
collection.author_corresponding_institution: School of Biopharmacy, China Pharmaceutical University, 639 Longmian Road, Nanjing 211198, China.
collection.abstract: Spatially organized tumor-stromal interactions contribute to metabolic remodeling and immune suppression in bladder cancer (BLCA). Using spatial transcriptional programs to define single-cell states, we identified a niche comprising SPINK1-high epithelial cells (E2) and TPM2-high cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) (C1). SPINK1 promoted tumor growth and myofibroblastic CAF programs, with EGFR and TGF-{beta} signaling implicated in tumor-CAF communication. Inferred metabolic reactions and spatial metabolite distributions supported a candidate circuit linking tumor-derived lactate to CAF oxidative metabolism and glutamine provision, followed by tumor glutamine utilization for reductive carboxylation and fatty acid synthesis. SPINK1 perturbation altered extracellular glutamine and lactate concentrations. Predicted chemokine interactions implicated C2/C3 CAFs in T cell recruitment, whereas the E2-C1 niche exhibited checkpoint and exhaustion-associated features. RHCG-positive tumor regions contained higher proportions of TOXCXCR4 cells among CD3 T cells, suggesting a possible association between ammonia handling and T cell dysfunction. In vivo, Spink1 loss attenuated tumor progression, increased cytotoxic CD8 T-cell infiltration, and enhanced tumor control during PD-1 blockade. These findings identify a spatially organized tumor-stromal niche associated with metabolic cooperation and immune restriction, supporting SPINK1 as a candidate therapeutic target in combination with immunotherapy.

collection.title: Evaluating novel sources of resistance to Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. cubense tropical race 4 (TR4) in a global banana diversity panel
collection.authors: Olave-Achury, C.; Ponndorf, D.; Chaparro Garcia, A.; Hall, A.; McGrann, G.; De Vega, J. J.
collection.abstract: Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. cubense tropical race 4 (Foc TR4) poses a major threat to global banana production, yet quantitative variation in resistance across Musa diversity remains poorly characterised. In this study, 21 accessions representing many of the major cultivated Musa groups and wild relatives were evaluated for their response to Foc TR4 under controlled-environment conditions. Significant variation in Foc TR4-associated corm discolouration was observed across the panel. Eight accessions had significantly less corm discolouration than the susceptible control Dwarf Cavendish: five were classified as resistant (all plants with more than 80% healthy corm area): Musa itinerans, M. schizocarpa, FHIA-02, FHIA-21 and the plantain Curare, and three as tolerant, which response was significantly different to the Dwarf Cavendish control but with some plants affected: M. ornata, Pelipita and Mai'a Maoli Koa'e. All accessions with only A genomes were susceptible or very susceptible, as were M. textilis and the B-containing triploids Pome (AAB) and Silver Bluggoe (ABB). Five of the seven accessions carrying at least one B genome were resistant or tolerant, suggesting that B-genome backgrounds merit wider screening as potential sources of resistance. These results identify valuable sources of resistance to Foc TR4 and provide a basis for banana breeding and further investigation of the genetic basis of resistance at the cultivar level.

collection.title: LORELEI sequence variation modulates lineage-dependent pollen tube reception in Brassicaceae
collection.authors: Jong, E.; Noble, J. A.; Alcaraz, M. J.; Hafidh, S.; Varghese, I.; Honys, D.; Lisi, G. P.; Beilstein, M. A.; Palanivelu, R.
collection.author_corresponding_institution: School of Plant Sciences, University of Arizona, Tucson, Arizona, 85721, USA
collection.abstract: Pollen tube reception (PTR) is essential for fertilization and can act as a prezygotic barrier in interspecific crosses. While core female components such as LORELEI (LRE) and FERONIA (FER) mediate conspecific PTR, their roles in heterospecific compatibility remain unclear. Here, we investigated how LRE sequence variation influences PTR outcomes with heterospecific pollen in Brassicaceae. In Arabidopsis thaliana, PTR frequently failed when ovules were pollinated with Arabidopsis lyrata or Sisymbrium irio, and loss of LRE or FER further increased pollen tube overgrowth in a pollen-species-dependent manner. Complementation of lre ovules with LRE orthologs showed distinct, donor-dependent effects: AlyLRE and SiLRE produced modest and variable improvements with A. lyrata pollen, whereas SiLRE consistently and markedly improved reception of S. irio pollen. Evolutionary analyses indicated relaxed purifying selection in the LRE lineage relative to its paralog LLG1 and nominated residues 47 and 120 as candidates for functional divergence. Consistent with this, the Lineage II-associated R120T substitution enhanced reception of S. irio pollen while partially reducing conspecific PTR. In addition, the ancestral-state E47P-R120G combination also improved heterospecific PTR without measurably compromising conspecific function. Together, these results indicate that LRE sequence diversification can modulate female-side compatibility with pollen tubes from different evolutionary lineages, potentially by altering how pollen tube-derived signals are sensed and transduced during reception.

collection.title: Daily-Academic: A Semantic Literature Discovery and Journal Tracking Platform for Biomedical Research
collection.authors: Grigoriadis, D.; Georgakopoulos-Soares, I.; Pavlopoulos, G.; Perdikopanis, N.
collection.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Informatics and Telecommunications, National and Kapodistrian University of Athens, Athens, Greece
collection.abstract: Objective: Biomedical researchers monitoring newly published literature rely on fragmented combinations of keyword alerts, manual database searches, journal subscriptions and repository portals. We aimed to develop and evaluate an integrated platform that unifies semantic literature discovery, journal monitoring and linked omics dataset exploration within a single researcher-oriented workflow, driven by a user profile that remains explicit and editable. Methods: Daily-Academic aggregates publication metadata from biomedical literature repositories and public omics resources and encodes titles and abstracts as dense semantic representations to support similarity-based retrieval beyond keyword matching. Recommendations are ranked by combining semantic relevance to the user profile with publication recency and journal-level preferences. The profile is derived from three user-supplied signals: a free-text statement of research interests, an optional link to the user's own publication record, and interaction history. Retrieval quality was assessed on an offline benchmark of 30 biomedical queries over a fixed corpus of 259,246 publications, comparing Daily-Academic with a lexical BM25 baseline and a PubMedBERT bi-encoder under pooled assessment with graded relevance judgements. Results: Query-level analysis indicated that the differences were distributed across queries rather than driven by a small subset. Conclusion: Integrating semantic retrieval into a unified discovery workflow with an inspectable user model improved the quality of top-ranked biomedical literature relative to established lexical and dense baselines. Because the benchmark is user-free, the adaptive component of personalisation was inactive and the ranking weights untuned; the observed advantage therefore reflects the semantic representation rather than adaptive personalisation. The platform is publicly available at https://www.daily-academic.com. Keywords: biomedical informatics, literature discovery, semantic retrieval, recommender systems, journal tracking, personalized feeds, scientific monitoring

collection.title: Charge-engineered nanohybrid coatings for microbial fouling resistance
collection.authors: Devadig, R.; Kandadai, V. A. S.; Jawaharraj, K.; Jasthi, B. K.; Gnimpieba, E.; Shagla, C.; Dalton, A.; McHugh, J.; Ajayan, P. M.; Tripathi, M.; Gadhamshetty, V.
collection.author_corresponding_institution: South Dakota School of Mines and Technology
collection.abstract: Microbial attachment is the gateway to biofouling and microbially influenced corrosion. Yet biocides and passive barrier coatings do not actively regulate the charged metal-microbe interface at which adhesion begins. Here we report a charge-engineered coating, a graphene thin-film nanohybrid (gTFN) on nickel (Ni) forming an asymmetric metal-graphene-metal junction, that suppresses cell attachment through interfacial charge redistribution rather than soluble toxicity. Against the model sulfate-reducing bacterium Oleidesulfovibrio alaskensis G20, gTFN combines an impermeable graphene scaffold, an immobilized low-leaching Ag cap and a serrated topology, reducing microbial surface coverage by 98%, increasing charge-transfer resistance 47-fold and lowering corrosion current 167-fold relative to Ni. Surface-potential mapping and density functional theory reveal interfacial dipoles that pattern the surface potential, while imaging shows graphene wrinkles channeling residual attachment. Transcriptomic profiling reveals downregulation of biofilm-associated and energy-metabolism genes. These results establish interfacial charge redistribution as an active antifouling and anticorrosion mechanism for controlling microbial biointerfaces.

collection.title: MetaEntropy: quantifying protein variability in complex viral mixtures via entropy
collection.authors: Jones, L. R.; Manrique, J. M.
collection.abstract: High-density sequence data has become commonplace in the study of complex viral mixtures from wastewater. Established algorithms are available for lineage deconvolution and labelling of clinically-elusive mutations. However, less attention has been paid to the quantification of translated amino acid diversity. We present MetaEntropy, a modular R package for assessing protein sequence variability and identifying sites under potential selection via Shannon entropy. MetaEntropy integrates utility functions for visualizing genome-wide and protein-specific variability, extracting nucleotide and amino acid mutation profiles, and identifying entropy hotspots. Despite being designed for wastewater surveillance, the package can also profile protein diversity from cross-sectional intra-patient data. However, it does not analyze population structure or quasispecies, for which several tools are available. By focusing on positional entropy, MetaEntropy bypasses the sequence constraints, computational overhead, and consensus-based variant loss typical of traditional haplotype reconstruction and multiple sequence alignment strategies. To balance sensitivity against neutral variation, the package evaluates entropy using a standard 20-class canonical amino acid scheme and a 7-class model based on traditional physicochemical properties. Calculated entropy values are normalized to a 0-1 scale, enabling direct comparisons of protein diversity across loci and sample strata. As proofs of concept, we employ MetaEntropy to detect well-known SARS-CoV-2 functional changes from wastewater data, and to explore tissue-specific heterogeneity in systemic infections. MetaEntropy is available from the Comprehensive R Archive Network (CRAN) at https://CRAN.R-project.org/.

collection.title: An Infected Cryopreserved Precision-Cut Lung Slice Model for Drug Susceptibility Testing in Pneumocystis murina Pneumonia
collection.authors: Pellegrino, M. R.; McLean, J. L.; Kottom, T.; Limper, A.
collection.abstract: Precision-cut lung slices (PCLS) preserve native three-dimensional lung architecture and cellular complexity, providing a valuable ex vivo platform for studying pulmonary host-pathogen interactions. However, existing PCLS infection models typically introduce microorganisms into previously uninfected tissue, while fresh PCLS prepared from infected lungs have limited experimental flexibility and scalability. To our knowledge, cryopreserved PCLS generated from lungs with an established in vivo pulmonary infection have not been described. Herein, we evaluated cryopreserved PCLS from mice with established Pneumocystis murina pneumonia (PCP) as an ex vivo platform for infection and therapeutic studies. PCLS were prepared from dexamethasone-immunosuppressed mice with established PCP, rested for 24 h, cryopreserved in a novel freezing medium for 12 days in liquid nitrogen, rapidly thawed, recovered for 24 h, and treated with pentamidine for 72 h. Viability was assessed in uninfected and PCP-infected PCLS before and after cryopreservation. Although post-thaw viability decreased in both groups, substantial viability was still retained, allowing further experimentation. qPCR showed that cryopreservation did not alter expression of the type I and type II alveolar epithelial markers podoplanin (Pdpn) and surfactant protein C (Sftpc) in either group. Importantly, pentamidine significantly reduced Pneumocystis mitochondrial small subunit (mtSSU) rRNA levels in thawed PCP-infected PCLS, demonstrating suitability for anti-Pneumocystis drug testing. These findings establish the first cryopreserved ex vivo PCP model using infected mouse PCLS, preserving endogenous fungal burden and infection-associated host responses while enabling flexible, scalable studies of Pneumocystis biology, host-pathogen interactions, therapeutic efficacy, and potentially other pulmonary infections.

collection.title: Beta-cell-derived urocortin-3 contributes to glucose-regulated somatostatin and glucagon secretion in the mouse pancreas
collection.authors: Vergara-Ucin, J.; Andersen, D. B.; di Giuseppe, G.; Mezza, T.; Rosenkilde, M.; Holst, J. J.
collection.abstract: Aims/Hypothesis. Glucagon secretion is impaired in both type 1 and type 2 diabetes. The mechanisms behind this dysregulation are incompletely understood. Urocortin-3 (UCN-3), a beta-cell-derived peptide, stimulates somatostatin (SST) secretion and may thereby regulate glucagon secretion. We investigated the mechanisms through which UCN-3 regulates pancreatic hormone secretion and examined the physiological contribution of endogenous UCN-3 to glucose-regulated hormone secretion. Methods. Pancreatic hormone secretion was studied using the isolated perfused mouse pancreas. The effects of exogenous and endogenous UCN-3 were investigated using selective antagonists of SST receptors (SSTR) and corticotropin-releasing hormone receptor 2 (CRHR2). In addition, the role of UCN-3 was examined in streptozotocin (STZ) treated mice. Results. Exogenous UCN-3stimulated somatostatin secretion and inhibited glucagon secretion in the mouse pancreas. Blockade of SSTRs completely abolished the glucagonostatic effect of UCN-3, demonstrating that inhibition of glucagon secretion is indirectly mediated through SST signaling. Moreover, CRHR2 antagonism prevented both UCN-3-induced SST secretion and inhibition of glucagon secretion, identifying CRHR2 as the key receptor mediating these effects. During acute glucose stimulation (3.5-10mM), CRHR2 antagonism reduced glucose-induced stimulation of SST and attenuated glucagon inhibition, indicating that endogenous UCN-3 participates in the acute islet response to hyperglycemia. However, during sustained hyperglycemia, CRHR2 antagonism reduced SST secretion without altering glucagon secretion. In STZ-treated mice, glucose-induced SST secretion was lost. Conclusions. Urocortin-3 regulated glucagon secretion indirectly through CRHR2-dependent stimulation of SST secretion. Endogenous UCN-3 contributes to the acute islet response to hyperglycemia, supporting a physiologically relevant beta-cell-to-delta-cell-to-alpha-cell paracrine axis in the mouse pancreas. This pathway is disrupted following beta-cell loss, suggesting a potential contribution to impaired islet hormone regulation in diabetes.

collection.title: Palmitic acid overload does not promote full-blown dysfunction in SGBS adipocytes which is reflected in their secretome
collection.authors: Angelini, S.; Stifani, G.; La Runa, G.; Cosenza, L. C.; Lodi, G.; Voltan, R.; Secchiero, P.; Castaldo, F.; Gessi, S.; Merighi, S.; Fernandez, M.; Bigot, A.; Wabitsch, M.; Cervellati, C.; Sanz, J. M.; Passaro, A.; Sergi, D.
collection.abstract: Background: Energy excess, and particularly long-chain saturated fatty acid (SFA) overload, are instrumental in promoting obesity and hampering metabolic health. However, SFA contribution to human adipocyte metabolic and endocrine dysfunction remains elusive. Nonetheless, we have already provided evidence that a 48-hour palmitic acid (PA) exposure is not sufficient to hamper Simpson-Golabi Behmel Syndrome (SGBS) adipocytes insulin signalling. Objective: This study aims at evaluating whether a 96-hour exposure to PA is able to disrupt SGBS adipocyte metabolic health and induce the release of a secretome capable of hampering insulin signalling in skeletal muscle cells. Methods: SGBS adipocytes were treated with either 1000 uM PA or bovine serum albumin (BSA) for 96 hours followed by the assessment of the NFkB signalling and the expression of genes associate with inflammation and adipocyte metabolic stress. Furthermore, adipocytes were labelled with BODIPY and lipid droplet as well as cell size semi-quantified using ImageJ. Insulin-induced phosphorylation of Akt and Akt substrate of 160 kDa (AS160) was assessed by Western Blot. The effect of PA on SGBS secretome was assessed by both ELISA as well as MILLIPLEX. Finally, human immortalised myotubes were co-cultured with BSA or PA-treated SGBS adipocytes for 24 hours followed by the assessment of insulin signalling at the Akt level. Results: PA did not activate the NFkB signalling pathway, but induced the expression of MCP-1 while tending to upregulate IL-6 mRNA levels. Despite 96-hour PA exposure leading to an increase in lipid droplet and cell size, this was not coupled with an impairment in insulin signalling. Nevertheless, this SFA promoted an increase in IL-6 and IL-8 secretion while tending to enhance the release of adiponectin by SGBS adipocytes. Finally, the secretome from PA-treated SGBS adipocyte did not impair insulin-induced phosphorylation of Akt relative to controls in myotubes. Conclusions: Thus, in the absence of the stromal vascular fraction, direct exposure of SGBS adipocytes to PA overload is not sufficient to elicit overt dysfunction. The absence of full-blown adipocyte dysfunction is reflected in the secretome of these cells which failed to disrupt skeletal muscle insulin signalling.

collection.title: Comparative transcriptomics reveals shared and context-dependent adaptations of bovine cells across culture systems for cultivated meat
collection.authors: Ribarski-Chorev, I.; Burghardt, M.; Tawil, S.; Gershkoviz, A.; Shpatz, D.; Schudy, G.; Beh Hamo, Y.; Gilad, Y.; Vainshtein, I.; Kfir, A.; Tuller, T.; Schlesinger, S.
collection.author_corresponding_institution: The Department of Animal Sciences, Robert H. Smith Faculty of Agriculture, Food, and Environment,  The Hebrew University of Jerusalem,  Rehovot 7610001, Israel
collection.abstract: Developing cell-culture systems for cultivated meat requires understanding how candidate cells respond to prolonged expansion and different growth environments. However, the extent to which bovine cells share transcriptional adaptations across these conditions, or retain responses specific to their origin and cellular state, remains unclear. Here, we systematically profiled bovine umbilical cord (BUC)- and adipose tissue (BAT)-derived mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) across different culture architectures, passage stages, and differentiation states, including immortalized BUC cells and satellite cells as a myogenic reference. We show that global transcriptomic variation is strongly associated with culture architecture, cell identity, and cellular state. Immortalization preserved several early-passage transcriptional features, particularly proliferation-related programs, while opposing selected changes associated with primary cell aging. Culture architecture induced distinct rather than uniform three-dimensional responses. Spheroid formation produced a pronounced transcriptional shift characterized by reduced proliferation-, chromatin-, and development-associated programs, alongside changes in extracellular-matrix organization, metabolism, and intracellular remodeling. Across primary umbilical cord-derived, adipose-derived, and myogenically induced umbilical cord-derived cells, scaffold-versus-plate comparisons revealed correlated but non-identical transcriptional responses. These involved changes in extracellular-matrix organization, adhesion, membrane trafficking, and developmental pathways, with endocytosis enriched across all three comparisons among the pathways examined. During myogenic induction, both satellite cells and BUC-derived cells exhibited muscle-related cytoskeletal and contractile programs, while scaffold culture further supported myogenic signatures in BUC-derived cells. These findings distinguish recurring culture-associated responses from transcriptional features tied to cell source and expansion history. They support evaluating cultivated-meat candidate cells in their intended culture systems, not solely under conventional plate conditions.

collection.title: Large-scale Nanopore sequencing resolves species diversity and distribution of European Ulva
collection.authors: van der Loos, L. M.; D'hondt, S.; Coulembier Vandelannoote, E.; Bafort, Q.; Casteleyn, G.; Akdogan Sirin, P.; Accoroni, S.; Ahsan, U.; Albert, G.; Arenas, F.; Armeli Minicante, S.; Aruci, E.; Bakratsas, G.; Balina, K.; Barboza, F. R.; Barda, I.; Bartolo, A.; Bartsch, I.; Becker, J.; Belattmania, Z.; Bellanti, G.; Bermejo, R.; Bernardi Aubry, F.; Bizien, A.; Blanfune, A.; Blomme, J.; Bo Rasmussen, M.; Boderskov, T.; Bonacic, K.; Bourgougnon, N.; Brazier, P.; Brodie, J.; Bruhn, A.; Bunker, F.; Burel, T.; Camus, J.; Canning-Clode, J.; Chemodanov, A.; Courtois de Vicose, G.; Cremades, J.; Dake, A.
collection.abstract: The green algal genus Ulva is widespread and ecologically important in European coastal ecosystems. However, species diversity and distributions remain poorly resolved due to phenotypic plasticity and historical taxonomic uncertainty. By adopting a large-scale sampling and barcoding effort, we provide a unique continent-scale assessment of Ulva species diversity and distribution. We developed a novel high-throughput Oxford Nanopore Technologies sequencing strategy, pooling 768 samples (eight 96-well plates) per run and sequencing tufA and ITS simultaneously. Nanopore barcoding was accurate and efficient, with 96.3% of samples yielding at least one informative marker. Consensus sequences showed 99.4-100% similarity to Sanger sequences. By analysing 3,657 samples from 30 countries, we identified 46 species with contrasting distribution patterns and substantially expanded their known geographic ranges. This includes numerous country-level first records and the first records of Ulva howensis outside Australia and U. meridionalis within the study area. Five non-indigenous Ulva species were also detected, including widespread occurrences of U. australis. However, 10 species could not be assigned to named taxa because suitable reference sequences were unavailable or unreliable, highlighting persistent taxonomic gaps in public databases. Our findings demonstrate the power of coordinated, high-throughput molecular surveys to resolve cryptic marine biogeography at continent scales. The resulting high-resolution spatial baseline facilitates the early detection of non-indigenous species and range expansions. It also enables coastal managers to monitor invasion pathways, evaluate ecosystem risks associated with opportunistic bloom-forming taxa, and detect climate-driven distribution shifts across European waters.

collection.title: ChIP-seq analysis of SMAD3 target genes in a sea anemone reveals symbiosis-dependent regulation through TGF-β signaling
collection.authors: Burleigh, O. L.; Dix, M. F.; Ruggeri, M.; Cui, G.; Aranda, M.; Weis, V. M.
collection.abstract: Background: Cnidarian-algal symbiosis underpins coral reefs, but elevated temperatures can disrupt it, causing bleaching. Bleaching activates host stress and immune pathways and disrupts symbiotic signaling and nutrient transfer. Among these pathways, the immunosuppressive cytokine transforming growth factor-{beta} (TGF-{beta}) promotes host tolerance of symbionts in cnidarians, but the genes regulated by its transcription factor, SMAD3, remain unknown. SMAD3 ChIP-seq and RNA-seq were used to identify putative targets in symbiotic and aposymbiotic Exaiptasia diaphana after 6 and 18 h of heat stress. Results: SMAD3 binding was highly specific to each combination of symbiotic state and heat treatment. Symbiotic state, not heat stress, drove most differential binding, with binding nearly always higher in symbiotic animals. Integration identified 625 putative targets differentially bound and expressed between symbiotic states. Differential binding between symbiotic states peaked at 18 h, when these targets made up the largest share of symbiosis-associated expression differences. Activation targets suggest SMAD3 supports symbiosis through the mucociliary surface, host control of nitrogen available to symbionts, uptake of symbiont-derived retinoids, and immunity. Repression targets, which outnumbered activation targets at 18 h, suggest SMAD3 limits canonical sterol transport, alters G protein-coupled receptor expression, and may reinforce its own activity by repressing negative regulators of TGF-{beta} signaling. Conclusions: SMAD3 appears to act as a bifunctional regulator whose binding is shaped primarily by symbiotic state. Its putative targets suggest roles in cnidarian symbiosis beyond immune suppression, including nutrient exchange and retinoid signaling. These findings provide a framework for TGF-{beta} function in cnidarian symbiosis and thermal stress.

collection.title: 2-hydroxyglutarate-dependent inhibition of TET2 is a molecular link between metabolic reprogramming and smooth muscle cell differentiation
collection.authors: Kwartler, C. S.; Esparza Pinelo, J. E.; Robin, A. M.; Richard, A.; Dosunmu, A. O.; Garcia Serrano, J.; Gonzalez Hernandez, A. D.; Krenz, H.; Chen, J.; Carrera, M.; Bornes, K. E.; Roy, S. S.; Chatthopadhyay, A.; Milewicz, D. M.; Gottlieb, E.
collection.author_corresponding_institution: The University of Texas Health Science Center at Houston
collection.abstract: Background: Smooth muscle cell (SMC) phenotypic modulation is accompanied by metabolic reprogramming, but the mechanisms linking metabolism to contractile gene expression remain unclear. We investigated whether 2-hydroxyglutarate (2-HG), an inhibitor of ?-ketoglutarate-dependent dioxygenases, links metabolic changes to regulation of ten-eleven translocation 2 (TET2) in Acta2R179C/+ SMCs Methods: Primary wild-type (WT) and Acta2R179C/+ mouse aortic SMCs were treated with nicotinamide riboside (NR), exogenous R&L-2-HG, or cholesterol. Endogenous accumulation of L-2HG was achieved by lentivuris-mediated knockdown (KD) of L2hgdh. We assessed contractile marker expression, cellular metabolism, TET2 chromatin occupancy, and DNA methylation and hydroxymethylation. L-2HG levels were assessed using liquid chromatography/mass spectroscopy. Carotid artery 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC) staining was assessed in mice after left carotid artery ligation. Results: Acta2R179C/+ SMCs have elevated 2-HG, reduced TET2 expression and chromatin occupancy, and lower 5hmC enrichment at CArG-containing SMC loci, consistent with repressed TET2 activity. NR boosts oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), reduces 2-HG in WT and mutant SMCs, increases TET2 expression and 5hmC enrichment, and reduces global 5-methylcytosine. Carotid artery 5hmC staining shows changes in the same direction, but group differences are not statistically significant. Exogenous L-2-HG attenuates NR-induced contractile marker expression in Acta2R179C/+ SMCs and also decreases contractile marker expression, reduces TET2 occupancy and 5hmC enrichment, and shifts WT SMC metabolism toward glycolysis, phenocopying the metabolic state of Acta2R179C/+ SMCs. Endogenous accumulation of L-2HG by L2hgdh KD reduces contractile markers in WT SMCS. Cholesterol reduces TET2 and contractile marker expression, decreases 5hmC enrichment, and increases global DNA methylation. Conclusions: These findings support a role for 2-HG in coupling metabolic state to epigenetic changes associated with SMC phenotypic modulation. NR-associated differentiation coincides with increased TET2 expression and DNA hydroxymethylation, identifying metabolic regulation of the SMC epigenome as a potential approach to preserving contractile gene expression.

collection.title: Extra-sheath transplantation of human retinal organoids (hROs): effects on visual recovery and retinal repair following optic nerve injury
collection.authors: Luo, Y.; Chen, X.; Kang, J.; Qin, H.; Kai, Y.; xu, H.
collection.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Ophthalmology, The First Affiliated Hospital of Army Medical University (Southwest Hospital)
collection.abstract: Traumatic optic nerve injury interrupts retinal ganglion cell output and can produce permanent visual disability, yet a therapeutic strategy that couples retinal protection with recovery of visual-pathway activity remains unavailable. Here, we evaluated human retinal organoid transplantation at the site of optic nerve crush in C57 mice. Human retinal organoids derived from embryonic stem cells were used at day 30 and showed retinal-lineage immunoreactivity together with spontaneous microelectrode-array activity. Across post-surgical days 7, 14, and 28, transplantation was associated with preservation of optic-disc appearance and ganglion cell layer thickness. The structural benefit became statistically distinguishable from the crush group at day 28 and remained incomplete relative to the uninjured or sham group. Serial RBPMS and TUJ1 immunostaining further supported attenuation of retinal ganglion cell body and neurite loss, while IBA1 staining indicated an altered microglial response. Full-field electroretinographic b-wave responses showed no detectable between-group differences, arguing against a major outer-retinal effect. In contrast, flash visual evoked potential P2 amplitude was higher in transplanted than in crush-only mice at all measured time points, consistent with improved visual-pathway responsiveness. Transplant recipients also showed enhanced optomotor responses across tested spatial-frequency and contrast conditions. Light-dark behavior shifted toward greater dark-compartment occupancy and activity, although this assay remains non-specific for visual recovery. Together, these findings support a model in which hROs transplantation at an optic nerve injury site promotes multi-level functional preservation after optic nerve crush. Definitive evidence for donor-derived circuit reconstruction will require graft tracing, synaptic validation, and prespecified electrophysiologic analyses.

collection.title: The genetic architecture of lipoprotein(a): simplicity, complexity, and mutability
collection.authors: Mukamel, R. E.; Rubinacci, S.; Kamitaki, N.; Handsaker, R. E.; Hujoel, M. L. A.; Tang, D.; McCarroll, S. A.; Loh, P.-R.
collection.author_corresponding_institution: Brigham and Women's Hospital and Harvard Medical School
collection.abstract: High levels of lipoprotein(a) (Lp(a)) increase risk of cardiovascular diseases. Lp(a) concentration is primarily determined (>80%) by genetic variation at LPA, particularly by its large, size-polymorphic kringle IV-2 (KIV-2) repeat. However, because variation of the KIV-2 repeat is difficult to measure, the precise ways that genetic variants at LPA and other loci determine Lp(a) levels have been unclear, especially in individuals of non-European ancestry. Here, we developed new computational techniques to accurately genotype KIV-2 variation in whole-genome-sequenced population cohorts. Applying these methods to UK Biobank (n=490,414) and All of Us (n=245,394) provided insights into the genetic determinants of Lp(a) and the mutational dynamics of the KIV-2 repeat, which we found expands or contracts intra-allelically once every [~]500 generations. Variation in Lp(a) levels among people of all genetic ancestries was accurately predicted by a single, transferable genetic model capturing cis-epistatic effects of KIV-2 length and protein-altering polymorphisms in LPA. Controlling for predicted effects of LPA alleles revealed an additional, highly polygenic contribution to Lp(a) variation: LPA-adjusted Lp(a) levels associated with genetic variation at over 300 loci (P<5x10-8), much like other blood lipids. These results elucidate the genetic architecture and mutational origins of Lp(a) variation, showing how detailed characterization of a largely monogenic trait can provide surprising insights for complex trait genetics.

collection.title: Longitudinal computer vision-based behavioural phenotyping of group-housed dogs for translational and welfare research
collection.authors: Sato, M.; Uthayavathanan, P.; Gutknecht, J.; Campa, A.; Lorimer, T.; Vazquez-Pianzola, P.; Almasi, K.; Item, L.; N'Gouan, D.; Sturman, O.; Richter, H.
collection.abstract: Continuous behavioural monitoring is essential for assessing animal welfare and individual behavioural variation, yet traditional observation-based methods are labour-intensive and prone to bias. Here, we developed a modular framework with computer vision for automated behavioural profiling of group-housed Beagles, integrating You Only Look Once (YOLO)-based models for pose estimation, individual identification, and enrichment detection. A ceiling-mounted infrared camera system enabled uninterrupted monitoring under standard kennel conditions. The identity-independent YOLO-POSE model achieved 99% precision, 97% recall, and an mAP50 of 0.98, while the YOLO classification model reached 95% accuracy for individual identification without external markers. Combining posture, identity, and environmental information enabled automated quantification of spatial use, locomotor activity, social interactions, corridor-oriented behaviour, drinking behaviour, and enrichment use. Overall, this framework captured distinct behavioural profiles of individual dogs from the same litter housed in the same kennel, which can be used to assess animal welfare and to evaluate environmental enrichments objectively. Together, we demonstrate a scalable and non-invasive approach for continuous individual behavioural profiling of group-housed dogs for computational ethology and translational research. By separating pose estimation from identity assignment, the framework enables flexible deployment across changing social groups and facilitates application to previously unseen individuals with minimal training.

collection.title: Improving Target-Adverse Event Association Prediction via Inverse Node Frequency Transformation to Mitigate Knowledge Graph Topological Bias
collection.authors: Egbelo, T. M.; Jeynes, J. C. G.; Kurt, Z.; Veettil, R. V.; Gillet, V. J.
collection.abstract: Motivation: Identifying significant associations between therapeutic protein targets and adverse events (AEs) is a critical component of drug safety assessment. To accelerate the process, machine learning methods have been developed to predict these associations as edges in network data integrating molecular interactions and other key biomedical knowledge. However, these networks often suffer from topological imbalances where a minority of "hub" nodes determine the predictive signal. This "topological" or "degree bias" can lead to poor performance on novel or understudied targets where safety inference is most needed. Results: We introduce Inverse Node Frequency (INF), a generally applicable node degree-based approach for mitigating topological bias. Employing an enriched biomedical knowledge graph and our own carefully curated target-adverse event associations, we apply INF as a normalisation procedure on a class of graph-derived features called metapaths and evaluate their resulting target-AE association prediction performance. Our results demonstrate that INF significantly improves the true positive rate (TPR/recall) for low-degree targets compared to the untransformed metapath features as well as a popular established normalisation method, while also achieving highly competitive hits@k, a ranking-based metric for knowledge graph-based inference. We also evaluated INF on an external set of target-AE associations never before used for modelling, on which INF also showed superior resilience compared to the two benchmarks.

collection.title: Ionic waves drive fluid flow by inducing spatiotemporal porosity variations in the brain interstitial space
collection.authors: Sarkar, D.; Mukherjee, S.
collection.abstract: We develop a model of interstitial fluid (ISF) dynamics in the brain driven by traveling ionic waves. The cortex is modeled as a 2D porous sheet with an absorbent matrix. A prescribed 10% sinusoidal porosity variation induces mean flow of O(1) {micro}m/s, even without an imposed pressure gradient. Including perivascular spaces (PVSs) increases the velocity and pressure gradient, and yields volumetric flux through arterial and venous PVSs, with maximum magnitude of 2 x 10-2 {micro}L min-1 mm-1. We show analytically, in the large-wavelength limit, that the porosity variation enters the pressure field as first- and second-order corrections. We then simulate a physiologically realistic spreading depolarization (SD) wave, finding that the induced porosity variation raises the mean ISF pressure to 4 mmHg, which falls to -0.7 mmHg during recovery. SD yields a peak velocity of O(10-2) {micro}m/s and a peak flux of 3 x 10-3 {micro}L min-1 mm-1, and transiently stalls the PVS-driven flow. Although the SD wave produces a larger porosity change than the prescribed wave, it evolves slowly and drives weaker flow.

collection.title: Koopman Analysis Reveals Collective Modes Governing Cellular Dynamics
collection.authors: Dutta, S.; Yu, W.; Zheng, Z.; Giri, A.; Xing, J.
collection.abstract: Living systems are complex nonlinear systems that operate far from thermodynamic equilibrium, and this nonlinearity makes their dynamics difficult to analyze. Several linearization techniques have been developed to address this problem, but most are local. Koopman operator theory is a powerful alternative that linearizes a system globally. Here we show that it not only achieves global linearization but also reveals collective modes that govern the dynamics of complex, out-of-equilibrium nonlinear systems. Applying the approach to whole-cell dynamical models, we find that these collective modes have physical and biological significance and relate to distinct processes in the cell cycle and in cell-state transitions. Collective and normal modes are widespread in many-body systems, particularly in condensed matter (e.g., magnons, phonons, hydrodynamic modes) and in macromolecular dynamics (e.g., normal mode analysis). By demonstrating that such modes also exist in cell-state transition dynamics, and in non-equilibrium nonlinear systems more generally, we offer a new theoretical-physics perspective on these systems. The collective modes separate into slow and fast modes. Long-term dynamics are governed by a few dominant slow modes that form a slow manifold of much lower dimension than the original state space. Thus, although the cell is a very high-dimensional system, its cell-cycle dynamics ultimately reduce to a low-dimensional space. Each mode comprises the coordinated behavior of groups of genes and reflects the structure of the underlying gene regulatory network. The modes can also be decomposed into terms that behave like damped harmonic oscillators, drawing an analogy between the modes of a nonlinear system and the normal modes of many-body systems. Finally, our analysis suggests that the dominant modes are closely associated with biological processes in the cell cycle, including mitosis, spindle checkpoint signaling, and DNA replication and repair.
